prompt.context: Rubber Bumper Co is a small family-owned producer of rubber products. It prides itself on producing a limited range of products but producing the highest quality on the market. In general, new products are introduced after much deliberation and careful market study. The company has recently appointed a new President who noticed decreasing profits over the last couple of years.
prompt.question: Rubber Bumper Co has hired our firm to fix the decline in profits. What are all of the areas that need to be examined in order to identify any major issues that should be a priority?

clarifying_info.q: What type of products do they sell?
clarifying_info.a: The company only sells two products: rubber bands and condoms.

clarifying_info.q: Is the company seeing similar declines in topline sales?
clarifying_info.a: Topline sales have remained relatively stable over the last 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is Rubber Bumper's market position?
clarifying_info.a: Rubber Bumper is the market leader in both of their product industries.

exhibits.title: Market volume by competitor, rubber bands and condoms 2011-2017
exhibits.shows: Two tables showing annual unit sales (rubber bands in millions of pounds; condoms in millions of units) broken out by competitor from 2011 to 2017

framework: Profitability breakdown: revenues vs. costs for each product line
Product mix analysis: relative contribution and trajectory of rubber bands vs. condoms
Industry trends: market size, growth rate, and competitive dynamics in each segment
Competitive positioning: market share trends for Rubber Bumper vs. rivals
Cost structure: variable costs, overhead, and margin comparison across factories
Capacity and operations: factory utilization, production constraints, and capital needs
Strategic options: potential pivots, investments, or exits for each product line

questions.prompt: Question 1: The analysts compiled the two market tables in Exhibit 1. What does this tell you?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) The rubber band market is essentially flat (30-32M lbs/year); (2) Max Rubber is steadily gaining share while Rubber Bumper's rubber band volume is declining from 4M to 2M lbs; (3) The condom market is growing strongly (~29% from 2011 to 2017, 350M to 450M units); (4) Rubber Bumper's condom volume grew rapidly from 1M to 10M units but plateaued after 2014 while the total market keeps growing; (5) The condom industry is more fragmented and smaller players collectively are gaining share. A great answer proactively asks why Rubber Bumper's condom growth has stalled while the industry continues to expand.

questions.prompt: Question 2: The two factories essentially run as separate P&Ls with no shared fixed costs. Build a quick profitability summary for each factory for the most recent year (2017).
questions.guidance: Candidate must convert rubber volume to unit count, then to revenue. Watch for unit-conversion step. Should note that total profits are comparable but condom margins are significantly higher (150% return on costs vs. ~67% for rubber bands). A great answer also questions why condom factory overhead is half that of rubber bands despite the condom market showing stronger demand.

math.setup: Rubber Band Factory: 2M lbs rubber sold (from Exhibit 1, 2017); 125 rubber bands per lb; boxes of 500 rubber bands sold at $20/box; $1/lb variable cost; $4M annual overhead. Condom Factory: 10M condoms sold (from Exhibit 1, 2017); 4-packs sold at $3/pack; $0.10/condom variable cost; $2M annual overhead.
steps: RB Revenue: 2M lbs x 125 rbs/lb = 250M rubber bands; 250M / 500 per box = 500K boxes; 500K x $20 = $10M
Condom Revenue: 10M condoms / 4 per pack = 2.5M packs; 2.5M x $3 = $7.5M
math.answer: Rubber band factory profit: $4M; Condom factory profit: $4.5M. Condom margin on costs: $4.5M profit / $3M total costs = 150%. Rubber band margin on costs: $4M profit / $6M total costs = 67%.

questions.prompt: Question 3: The condom factory is at capacity and is about half the size of the rubber band factory. The President wants to evaluate whether to convert the rubber band factory to produce condoms (assume a factory can only make one product). Should Rubber Bumper convert the plant?
questions.guidance: A weak answer simply compares $4.5M vs $4M profit and recommends conversion. A strong answer accounts for: (1) opportunity cost of being offline for 1 year (lost rubber band contribution), (2) the $2M CapEx, (3) the incremental annual profit gain from the larger factory, and (4) the 4-year payback requirement. Candidate should also flag timing: payback occurs in year 3 (1 year offline + 2 years of higher profit), which is within the 4-year threshold. Additional second-level insights are encouraged.

math.setup: Conversion takes 1 year offline, costs $2M CapEx. No tax benefits from CapEx depreciation, no cost of capital. Overhead remains the same at $4M. Bigger plant can produce 2x the condom volume of the smaller plant. Rubber band demand has stabilized at 2M lbs/year. Company payback period: 4 years.
steps: Opportunity cost (1 year offline): lost rubber band contribution = Revenue - Variable Cost = $10M - $2M = $8M (overhead paid regardless, not an incremental cost)
Total cost of project: $8M opportunity cost + $2M CapEx = $10M
Bigger factory condom production: 2x current smaller factory = 2 x 10M condoms = 20M condoms (at current capacity)
Bigger factory condom contribution (ignoring overhead which is a wash): 20M condoms / 4 per pack x $3/pack - 20M x $0.10 = $15M - $2M = $13M
Current rubber band contribution from bigger factory: $10M - $2M = $8M
Incremental annual benefit from switching: $13M - $8M = $5M per year
Payback: $10M total cost / $5M per year = 2 years of operation; plus 1 year offline = 3 years total to payback
Conclusion: 3 years < 4-year payback threshold, so project meets the hurdle rate.
math.answer: Payback in year 3 (1 year offline + 2 operating years). Project meets the 4-year payback requirement. Recommendation: proceed with conversion.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some of the risks involved with converting the rubber band factory to produce condoms?

categories.name: Demand/Market assumptions
ideas: Assumes Rubber Bumper can immediately sell 3x the condoms it sells today (scale-up may take time)
Assumes rubber band demand will not rebound; if it does, the idle plant opportunity cost is understated
The bigger plant may be underutilized if condom sales growth stalls again as it did post-2014

categories.name: Competitive and industry risk
ideas: Condoms are less of a commodity than rubber bands; higher advertising and brand investment may be required to compete at scale
Regulatory/political risk: changes to sex education policy or contraception regulation could reduce demand
More fragmented condom market means more competition from nimble smaller players

categories.name: Business and financial risk
ideas: Loss of diversification: exiting rubber bands concentrates all revenue in one product line
Legal and liability risk is higher in contraception than rubber bands (product liability, recalls)
Sunk costs if market conditions shift during the 1-year conversion period

categories.name: Operational and people risk
ideas: Employees may be unwilling to manufacture condoms (cultural or personal objections)
Manufacturing processes differ; workforce may require retraining
1-year timeline for refurbishment may overrun, extending the offline period

recommendation: Rubber Bumper should convert the rubber band factory to produce condoms
The project meets the 4-year payback threshold, paying back in year 3
Condom margins are significantly superior (150% vs. 67% return on costs) and the market continues to grow
The rubber band segment is structurally declining with Rubber Bumper losing share to Max Rubber
risks: Inability to scale condom sales 3x quickly enough to achieve projected contribution
Rubber band demand rebound would increase the true opportunity cost
Regulatory or political changes affecting contraception demand
Increased legal/liability exposure in the contraception category
next_steps: Validate that distribution channels and retail relationships can absorb 20M condoms annually before committing
Develop a brand/advertising investment plan to compete in the more fragmented condom market
Assess workforce willingness and retraining requirements for the converted factory
Explore whether exiting rubber bands entirely is optimal or whether a licensing/sale of the rubber band business is possible
